note: Every verdict rendered against real third-party code. TP = we reported a real defect. FP = we reported something that was not one. Sourced entries name the repository, file and line so any verdict can be re-checked.

entries.shape: .extract() on something that is not an archive
entries.why: OpenTelemetry propagation.extract() and an OAuth claims extractor. Neither touches an archive.
A lint rule comparing an AST node kind against an enum member. The identifier carries "token"; the value is a discriminant.
Plain type coercion reported as CWE-697 HIGH. A filename and an error code are not credentials. IGNF suppressed this rule 15 times over exactly this.
Substring match on "token". The value is an algorithm name, not a credential.
Optional chaining defeats sanitizer detection, so the MORE defensive spelling is reported as CWE-79 CRITICAL. Blocks an upgrade PR to seven Adobe repos.
Every generated TypeORM migration carries this field. The trailing timestamp makes the literal look high-entropy.
Three findings on a fixture whose only claim was a safe algorithm allowlist. Hardening advice reported as defects — the one FP in the scored corpus.
The only name heuristic in the suite with no option to override it. A pg.Pool named db is missed; carpoolService is flagged.
A linter rebuilding a regex from an AST node’s own flags. No attacker input exists.

entries.shape: a computed-key WRITE whose key is locally derived
entries.why: Not 4,286 shapes and not seven decisions — ONE. The rule reports every computed-key write and stays silent on every read, which is the correct half of the line (prototype pollution needs a write). The open question is whether a write should report without evidence that the key is attacker-controlled. Every one of the seven head shapes has a locally derived key: a loop counter, Object.keys of a sibling, a tag name.
entries.precedent: node-security/no-timing-unsafe-compare, inverted to require an attacker-controlled operand

entries.why: Gates five HTTP endpoints. CWE-208.

entries.shape: Math.random() building a device pairing code
entries.why: The code is the map key that claims a pairing challenge. Predictable generator, 5-minute window. CWE-338.
Gates controller registration, the privileged role. The same file already used timingSafeEqual elsewhere.

entries.shape: signedPayload !== hmacSignature in a webhook guard
entries.why: KYC webhook signature verification. The guard had no test of any kind.
yauzl validates entry NAMES; nothing validated the link TARGET. Verified by building malicious zips: only this case escaped.

entries.shape: app.enable('trust proxy') behind an IP allowlist
entries.why: req.ip becomes attacker-controlled, bypassing authorizeIPAddress. Disclosure drafted, not sent.

entries.shape: every CallExpression treated as a promise
entries.why: One rule shipped twice by opposite constructions and the same defect. maintainability returned true for every CallExpression and said so in its own comment. reliability used a denylist of ~120 synchronous names, so everything it had not heard of was a promise. Together 11,866 of 20,009 findings — 59% — on lines like <div className={clsx("col")} />, require("./tree.svg") and const { siteConfig } = useDocusaurusContext(). Both now require evidence from the file itself; both went to 0 on the same 200 files.

entries.shape: a number that is already named, and a number that is data
entries.why: The largest source of findings once no-unhandled-promise was fixed. Classified over 120 TypeScript files: 290 of 735 (39%) were inside an all-numeric array literal — coordinates and colour matrices, which are data — and 246 (33%) were the initialiser of a named const reached through a type assertion or all-literal arithmetic. The rule already exempted `const FOO = 42`, but only as a DIRECT initialiser, so `180 as Degrees` and `10 / 1.5` walked past it. Reporting those contradicts the rule's own fix, which is to give the number a name. 735 → 428 on the same files; the remainder is `clamp(tolerance * height, 5, 80)` and `Math.max(GAP, 15)`, which are magic and should report.

entries.shape: a function passed as an argument, and an object-literal method
entries.why: The rule kept a LIST of callback-taking hosts — array methods, .then, setTimeout — and reported every callback to a host it had not heard of. `describe`/`it`/`test` were on no list, so every block in every spec file reported: 1,415 findings across two small repositories. Adding the test frameworks would have been the same mistake one entry larger; the survivors were `chrome.storage.onChanged.addListener` (`addEventListener` was listed, `addListener` was not) and `defineBackground`, a framework entry point no list would ever contain. Replaced with the structural fact: an argument cannot be moved to module scope without changing what it is an argument to, and neither can an object-literal method. 1,415 → 145, and the survivors are genuine nested helpers.

`collectReferences` walked `for (const key in node)`, which includes `parent` — a link back UP the tree. So "which names does this body use" was really "which names appear anywhere in the file": an arrow whose entire body is `42` collected `helper, outer`, appeared to capture its enclosing scope, and never reported. Only the `function` declaration form ever fired, which is why the rule looked like it worked. Arrows are the dominant modern form, so the rule was missing most of what it exists to find. A coverage fixture had documented the bug as intended behaviour: "function expressions assigned to variables reference their own binding through the parent chain and are treated as capturing".
